title: travel notes of a sensitive system
content:
meta-notes on what traveling does to my system — before, during, and after

I just returned from three weeks in China — and I want to write about the meta of traveling; how extremely disruptive traveling can feel — how it shakes up your insides, thrashes open your windows and rearranges all the furniture within the house of your being, and leaves you wandering and dazed, like a lost rabbit in your own home.

at least, that’s what traveling does for me — being in a different place completely overloads my system and makes me feel semi-poreous and transculent, like a jellyfish. I wake up empty, I wake with amnesia, I wake up and I completely forget who I am. I feel more plant than a human; like a tumbleweed drifting in the wind. if I’m not prepared for these feelings, traveling always induces a mild, grasping panic.

but, this time around, I was prepared. I was lucid. I took notes. I was honest about my psychic capacity. I was attuned and waiting for inevitable shifts, like feeling tectonic plates shifting underneath my feet. I want to share some notes and observations with you, here.


recognizing my sensitive system

I am not sure what other word to use — than “sensitivity.” by sensitive, I mean hyper-absorptive and aware, easily affected by every ripple and movement, stirred by the atmosphere in a room, by energy, by things said and left unsaid.

I mean that it takes extra effort to separate what’s mine — versus what I’m picking up from the people and environment around me. it takes days to wash away the feeling of a place, or the energy of a person. everything leaves an imprint on my mind, and without space to integrate, my being feels like an over-soaked sponge, or a carnivorous flower, or, at worse, the blue screen of death. everything seizes the imagination — even if I don’t realize it, until later.

sensitivity isn’t the same as emotionality, or reactivity — though it can manifest as that. it isn’t about fragility. it means that my system’s processing is fine tuned. it (seems to) pick up more than the average system does. everything feels potentially disruptive. boundaries feel both both necessary and sometimes, extremely difficult.

I use to think that this was a problem.

I used to want to be more… hardy, more sturdy, more nonchalant, more unaffected. I wanted to be able to work while I travel, like a “normal” person. I used to resent the exhaustion and emotional turmoil that would trail me afterwards for days, like a sulking shadow. I used to berate myself, to tell myself to get up, to keep up the pace, don’t waste time being so overwhelmed…

I don’t talk to myself like that anymore. these days, I see that a sensitive processing system is one of my greatest gifts, and I’m honoring it. this is what I teach in my course, creative systems, and this is what I try my best to practice, everyday.

the first thing I’m doing — here, in writing this down — is acknowledging it.



how I feel before departure

extreme inertia, heaviness, and resistance — before this particular trip, I felt extreme inertia. what I desired most was the opposite of travel — I wanted to hide in bed, to curl up on my couch, to crawl into a time portal and not move for 7 days. instead, I made myself do things — go to the park, run errands, visit the islands with K & L. my body didn’t feel ready to go, and parts of me resisted and cried and threw tantrums, like a sulking teenager. I let myself feel all of this, and K is very gentle with me.

the pressure of unfinished things — in the week leading up to departure, I felt the mounting pressure of a pile of unfinished work, incomplete circles, new ideas and seeds germinating that haven’t had a chance to grow (see my soon seeds). I felt anxiety about them — like, what if I don’t feel excited about these when I return? what if I return as a different person, and I lose all this momentum I built? what if I fall behind on the energy I had? what if it takes me a long time restart?

(all these what-ifs turned out to be true — but in a good way).

a mind making up new problems — my mind came up with new and urgent problems that needed solving. should I buy some last minute gifts for my relatives? should I cut my hair before I go? am I possibly pregnant?!? (yes, no, and no) I bring awareness to the realization that my mind is trying to keep me safe by trying to exercise its problem solving muscles.

riding a sudden gust of wind — then, 24 hours before my flight, I started packing. the act of packing rearranges my energy, makes the voyage feel imminent and real. I felt a gust of wind lift me off the ground. that day of my departure, the weather was perfect, cool blue and crisp. I found myself in the mood to travel 5,000 miles.



how I felt during travels

the feeling of total disembodiment — the first few days after arriving, I felt like an answering machine version of myself. I felt like my soul had left my body — I’m a clear vessel, an empty glass bottle with nothing in it. I’m a reflecting pool, holding reverbrations of smells, sounds, tastes, and colors.

given the density with which I usually inhabit myself in my home environment, this contrast feels strange and stark. it feels like my inner world has retreated, like a snail, and I’ve become only a shell. I am absent from myself, I am just a sensing body, continuously calibrating to the environment.

defining & practicing the bare minimum containers — the bare minimum during this particular trip was writing down, in two little microbook/zine booklets — (a) what I did today (green book) and (b) how I felt about it (red book). I filled one tiny page in each book — just before going to sleep, every night — jotted sentence fragments, like fish hooks for my memory.

of course, in my ideal travel experience, I would keep a travel sketchbook or writing notebook, and fill them to the brim with insightful, brilliant observations and rich watercolor paintings each day. it took me a long time to acknowledge that traveling is so exhausting for me that I usually don’t have the bandwidth for that. my system doesn’t crank out things simultaneously while experiencing them.

that is — digesting a day is a very different process than sensing/absorbing/living a day.

this particular trip was full of family obligations, complicated emotions, over-saturated sensory experiences, and very little alone time — so, defining my bare minimum processing container was essential.

small moments of spaciousness — after a few days in my new destination, I’ll feel my first moments of spaciousness, like my system is no longer in survival/hyper-vigilant / absorption mode. I can feel it my body, wanting more movement, wanting to stretch or do yoga before bed. my body is calling me back — asking me to reinhabit it deliberately. I can feel it in flickering, whispering insights that come to me, while waiting for the light to change, or while sitting in a taxi looking out the window. it arrives in the tiny moments between things.

anxiety pattern: filling the empty spaces — a pattern I noticed during all of my travels is that, after multiple over-satured days, the first spacious day will come with a wave of anxiety. my mind is overactivated — so even when it’s not overwhelmed, it panics and looks for something to feel overwhelmed about. recognizing that this is a pattern gave me great relief.

hidden shapes emerging with bursts of clarity — sometime near the last third of my travels, something happens. I can feel that my travels have caused a rearrangement of the pieces of my life. there are secret things happening, simmering, and processing in the background periphery of my awareness.

I watch the new arrangement of my life reveal itself to me, slowly. or, in bright, blinding flashes. I catch glimpses of certain things become startlingly clear — what I desire, what I need to do next, where I go from here, what life is asking of me now, how I relate to X, Y, or Z. things that felt fuzzy or swampy before this trip suddenly feel obvious and crystallized, like glimmering ice sculptures, here for a brief moment.

then, in the liminal moments (plane rides, slow mornings with coffee and a journal), I might touch my mind and feel an explosion of ideas falling out of it.



how I feel upon returning

alien exhaustion and total grief - I don’t think most travels are this emotionally intense, but going to China always leaves me with a grief that feels deeper than my consciousness can hold or comprehend — something old, transcendent, and inter-generational. I try to be very gentle with myself: full permission to sleep twelve hours, lots of spontaneous crying, and very little external obligations for a few days. I can feel that it’s not just me traveling — I’m also carrying my inner child self, all my past selves, and all my future selves with me, there and back again.

a disembodied stranger in my own life - the first few days, I feel (am still feeling right now) like a foreigner in my own life. I can’t do much other than tend to the animal needs of my body, and maybe pick up the fragments of myself and try to make something new from it. I try to conjure the clarity I felt during the last days of my trip. I look at my corkboard, my notes, my systems and feel like I need to start everything over from scratch, to make new containers for everything. I’ve been rearranged into an unfamiliar new shape, and I need new vessels to hold me.

the slow work of integration - I wrote down where I left off in my work projects — but I know better than to just hit the “resume” button and pick up from there. I can’t.

something has shifted, even if I don’t have the words to describe it yet. I can’t do much other than navigate the return much like I navigated my travels — step by step, slowly, asking my system what it needs to feel supported. this is in part what I learned and taught in creative systems, and it’s a practice I hold myself accountable to, everyday.

it’s difficult and filled with all kinds of discomfort, but I always emerge from it as if out of a wormhole, like I’ve traveled light years ahead and saw a glimpse of my future. I’ve changed, my inner parts are rearranging, like tectonic plates. now I’m here, waiting for the rest of my life to catch up.
